1240.title: The Gita at Walden
1240.hook: he bathed his mind in the Bhagavad Gita and imagined Walden's water mingling with the Ganges (Walden 16)
1240.howItsDone: Hindus read the Bhagavad Gita as scripture; Thoreau, writing as a reader from outside the tradition, describes bathing his mind in it each morning and picturing Walden's water mingling with the Ganges.

segments.voice: Yesterday, winter animals: owls, barking foxes, chickadees at the corn, and one trembling hare. Your line was winter life.

What could a small New England pond have to do with a river on the other side of the earth? In the winter Thoreau describes, an ice company came to Walden with horses, saws and long tools, cutting the frozen pond into blocks and stacking them high on the shore. The ice would be shipped, he tells us, to hot cities a world away. He watched them work. Then he went back to his cabin, his book and his well. And somewhere between the ice saws and the bucket, an answer arrived.
screen: `ICE CUTTERS ON THE POND.` → `SHIPPED TO HOT CITIES.` → `A POND AND A FAR RIVER.`

segments.voice: First, the book. Near the end of The Pond in Winter, Thoreau tells us what he reads in the morning: "In the morning I bathe my intellect in the stupendous and cosmogonal philosophy of the Bhagvat Geeta." That's his spelling of the Bhagavad Gita, the Hindu scripture where Krishna counsels the warrior Arjuna, whose dropped bow you met on day seven hundred twenty-four. Notice the verb. Not study, not skim: bathe, the way you'd step into the pond. Second, the well. He puts down the book and goes to his well for water, and there, in his imagination, he meets the servant of a Brahmin priest who sits in his temple on the Ganges reading the Vedas. They draw water, he says, from the same well, and their buckets grate together. A scripture read at dawn has turned a chore into a meeting. Third, the ice. Thoreau thinks of the blocks cut from Walden and shipped to hot cities in India, among other places, and writes: "The pure Walden water is mingled with the sacred water of the Ganges." It's a picture of water traveling. It's also ideas traveling the other way, from the Ganges to a cabin in Massachusetts. Fourth, what he's doing. Thoreau doesn't claim the Gita as his, or say what Hindus should make of it. He treats it as a neighbor's well he's been allowed to drink from. A line from far away came into his ordinary morning and changed the size of it. His small pond, read beside a great river, didn't feel small anymore.
screen: `I BATHE MY INTELLECT.` · `THE SERVANT AT THE WELL.` · `WALDEN WATER IN THE GANGES.` · then, large: `A NEIGHBOR'S WELL.`

If nothing comes, borrow Thoreau's: the pure Walden water is mingled with the sacred water of the Ganges. Let the line sit in you like water, without analyzing it, a morning bath.

1241.title: Spring at Walden
1241.hook: the thawing sand bank flows like leaves and veins; spring is a resurrection (Walden 17)
1241.howItsDone: Readers of Walden's Spring chapter often take the thawing sand bank and the pond's opening as images of renewal, watching for the first signs of new life at the end of a hard season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita at Walden: a morning bath in a far scripture, and pond water mingled with the Ganges. Your line was the Ganges and Walden.

A railroad cut, late in winter. Steep banks of sand and clay on either side of the tracks, still half frozen: the kind of place you walk past on the way to town without a glance. Thoreau stopped. As the sun warmed the bank, the frost let go, and the wet sand began to slide down the slope in little rivers. As it flowed, it made shapes: branching, lobed, like leaves and vines and the veins in a hand. He stood and watched a sand bank turn into a forest.
screen: `A RAILROAD CUT IN LATE WINTER.` → `THE SAND BEGINS TO FLOW.` → `LEAVES AND VEINS.`

segments.voice: First, the sand bank. In the chapter called Spring, Thoreau spends pages on that thawing slope, and says few things gave him more delight. The sand flows into forms like leaves, like lichens, like coral, like the paws of animals and the inside of a body. It's mud, drawing the shapes of living things. Second, his conclusion, short and startling: "There is nothing inorganic." The earth, he says, isn't a dead thing with life sitting on top of it. It's alive all the way through, a living poetry, the leaves of a tree still being written. Third, the pond. The ice on Walden breaks up, the water opens, the first birds come back, and he writes: "Walden was dead and is alive again." Readers who know the Bible may hear an echo of the father in the parable of the prodigal son, the story from day eighty-three, who says in the King James text that his son "was dead, and is alive again." Thoreau doesn't explain the echo. He just lets the pond come home. Fourth, why it matters. A thaw is not a sudden miracle. It's slow, and messy, and mostly mud at first. Thoreau stood in the mud and saw resurrection anyway. For him, spring wasn't only a season. It was a sign that what looks finished can begin again. You don't have to wait for April to watch for that. Maybe something in your own life is half frozen right now, and somewhere at its edge, the sand is starting to move.
screen: `THE SAND BANK FLOWS.` · `THERE IS NOTHING INORGANIC.` · `DEAD AND ALIVE AGAIN.` · then, large: `THE THAW BEGINS IN MUD.`

segments.voice: If you can see outside, look for one sign of new growth, a bud, a shoot, a fresh leaf, moss in a crack; whatever the season, something somewhere is starting. If not, turn inward: find one thing in your life that has felt frozen, and look along its edge for the first small movement, a softer word, a little more energy, a door a crack open. Don't force it; just notice the thaw.
Spring at Walden. Thoreau watched a thawing sand bank flow into leaves and veins, and wrote, Walden was dead and is alive again. Today's word.
Your line: the thaw. It starts small, and it starts in the mud. Until tomorrow.

1242.title: A different drummer
1242.hook: if someone doesn't keep pace with others, perhaps they hear a different drummer
1242.carry: perhaps the slow one hears a different drummer
1242.howItsDone: Readers often take Thoreau's different drummer as a call to patience with people who move at another pace, and as permission to follow a rhythm of their own without being rushed.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Spring at Walden: a thawing sand bank drawing leaves and veins, and a pond that was dead and is alive again. Your line was the thaw.

A group of friends on a trail. The others are already at the bend, checking the time. One is still back by the creek, crouched, looking at something in the water. Someone calls his name. Someone sighs. And the question nobody says out loud starts to form: what is wrong with him? Near the very end of Walden, Thoreau takes up exactly that person, the one who falls behind. His answer may not be the line it first sounds like.
screen: `ONE FRIEND FALLS BEHIND.` → `WHAT IS WRONG WITH HIM?` → `THOREAU ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: From Walden's last chapter, called Conclusion: "If a man does not keep pace with his companions, perhaps it is because he hears a different drummer. Let him step to the music which he hears, however measured or far away." First, who it's about. It's easy to hear a motto for yourself: march to your own beat. But Thoreau writes about someone else, the one lagging behind, from the companions' side. It's a sentence about how to look at the slow one. Second, the word perhaps. He doesn't say the slow one is a genius. Perhaps there's music you can't hear. It's a small, generous doubt that stops you before you decide what's wrong with someone. Third, the music is real but faint: however measured or far away. The drummer might be slow, or distant, and the person hearing it might not be able to explain it either. Fourth, the hurry. Just before this, Thoreau asks, "Why should we be in such desperate haste to succeed and in such desperate enterprises?" Just after, he says it isn't important that a person ripen as fast as an apple tree or an oak. "Shall he turn his spring into summer?" So the line isn't a slogan about standing out. It's a plea for time. Some people ripen late, or walk to a rhythm from far off, and the kindest thing their companions can do is let them.
screen: `ABOUT THE ONE WHO FALLS BEHIND.` · `PERHAPS.` · `MEASURED OR FAR AWAY.` · then, large: `SHALL HE TURN HIS SPRING INTO SUMMER?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose speed bothers you: a child who dawdles, a coworker who takes forever to decide, a parent who tells the story slowly. Hold them without fixing anything, and try Thoreau's word on them: perhaps they hear something you don't, perhaps their spring isn't ready to be summer. You don't have to agree with their pace; just let it be theirs for now.

Your line: perhaps the slow one hears a different drummer. The music may be far away. See you tomorrow.

1243.title: Give me truth
1243.hook: Thoreau: rather than love, money, fame, give me truth
1243.carry: truth before love, money and fame
1243.tomorrow: the sun is a morning star
1243.howItsDone: Readers of Walden often hold this line up as Thoreau's case for sincerity: saying what is actually so, even when the expected answer would be more comfortable.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one who falls behind on the trail, and Thoreau's generous perhaps. Your line was perhaps the slow one hears a different drummer.
screen: `PERHAPS THE SLOW ONE HEARS A DIFFERENT DRUMMER.`

segments.voice: Love. Money. Fame. Set them on a table in front of a stranger, ask them to pick one, and you'd learn a lot about the stranger. A love song picks the first. A business plan, the second. A talent show, the third. A few pages from the end of Walden, Thoreau pushes all three aside and asks for something that doesn't fit on the table at all. It's one short sentence, and it puts love on the losing side.
screen: `LOVE. MONEY. FAME.` → `PICK ONE.` → `THOREAU PUSHES ALL THREE AWAY.`

segments.voice: The sentence, from Walden's Conclusion: "Rather than love, than money, than fame, give me truth." First, the shock of the list. Money and fame are easy to set aside in a book about a cabin. But love? He doesn't say love is bad. He says that if he had to choose, he'd take truth first, maybe because love built on a pretense isn't quite love. Second, a dinner. Right after the line, he tells of a table with rich food, plenty of wine and attentive service, where sincerity and truth were missing. He went away hungry. A full plate, and he left hungry. That's how he measures a meal: not by what was served, but by whether anyone was honest at it. Third, what truth means to him here. A little earlier in the chapter he writes, "Say what you have to say, not what you ought. Any truth is better than make-believe." For Thoreau, truth isn't mainly a fact you look up. It's the difference between a real life and a performed one. Fourth, the cost. Choosing truth over love, money and fame means some rooms get colder, and some tables you leave early. Thoreau seems to accept that. He'd rather go home hungry than stay full on make-believe. Readers are free to argue with him, but the line is plain about where he stood.

segments.voice: Let one place come to mind where you say what you ought instead of what you have to say: a meeting, a family dinner, a friendship where something has gone unsaid. Don't rehearse a speech; just find the one true sentence underneath, short and kind, and say it silently a few times. Notice how it sits.

1244.title: The sun is a morning star
1244.word: The sun is a morning star
1244.hook: the sun is but a morning star; there is more day to dawn (Walden 18)
1244.howItsDone: Readers often return to the last lines of Walden as a morning reading: a reminder to be awake for the day that is actually arriving, and that more of it is still to come.

segments.voice: Yesterday: truth ahead of love, money and fame, and a rich table Thoreau left hungry. Your line was give me truth.

An old kitchen table made of apple-tree wood. Years of meals, elbows, spilled milk. Then one day the family hears a gnawing inside it, and a bug chews its way out of the dry wood, alive and beautiful. The egg, the story goes, had been laid in the living tree long before it became a table, and it waited all that time. Thoreau tells this on the last pages of Walden as a little resurrection. Then he ends the book with a few short sentences about the dawn.
screen: `AN OLD APPLE-WOOD TABLE.` → `A GNAWING SOUND.` → `LIFE OUT OF DRY WOOD.`

segments.voice: Walden's last lines: "The light which puts out our eyes is darkness to us. Only that day dawns to which we are awake. There is more day to dawn. The sun is but a morning star." First, too much light. A light bright enough to blind you is, to you, the same as dark. Some truths arrive too big to see all at once. Second, the day you're awake for. A sunrise happens whether you notice or not, but only that day dawns to which we are awake. The calendar can say morning while a person is still asleep inside. Third, more day to dawn. After a whole book of mornings at the pond, he says the day isn't finished arriving. Fourth, the sun is but a morning star. A morning star is the bright point you see before sunrise, a sign the day is near. Thoreau takes the biggest light there is and calls it only a sign of a brighter day still on its way. It's a strange, hopeful ending: no summary, no moral, a sunrise demoted to a herald, and the bug in the table still fresh in mind, life that waited in dry wood and came out when it was ready.
screen: `LIGHT THAT PUTS OUT OUR EYES.` · `ONLY THE DAY WE'RE AWAKE TO.` · `MORE DAY TO DAWN.` · then, large: `THE SUN IS BUT A MORNING STAR.`

1245.title: Why he left
1245.hook: he left the woods because he had several more lives to live (Walden 18)
1245.howItsDone: Readers often take Thoreau's reason for leaving Walden as permission to close a good chapter on purpose, before it hardens into habit, and to treat a life as several lives in turn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Walden's last lines: only the day we're awake to dawns, and the sun is but a morning star. Your line was more day to dawn.

Why would anyone walk away from the place he wrote a whole book loving? He built the cabin with his own hands. He sounded the pond through the ice. The bean rows, the loon, the ant war, the thaw. Then he packed up and went back to town. Readers still ask: if the woods were so good, why leave? Thoreau saw the question coming, and in his last chapter he answers in two plain sentences that sound less like an apology than a doorway.
screen: `HE BUILT IT. HE LOVED IT.` → `THEN HE LEFT.` → `TWO SENTENCES OF ANSWER.`

segments.voice: "I left the woods for as good a reason as I went there. Perhaps it seemed to me that I had several more lives to live, and could not spare any more time for that one." First, as good a reason. Back in year one, this path met the reason he gave near the start of the book: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately." So leaving gets the same respect as going. Not a failure or a retreat; the same deliberate choice, pointed the other way. Second, several more lives. Not one life with a detour at a pond, but several, one after another, and Walden was one. That's a roomy way to see a lifetime: chapters that are each whole. Third, the warning right after. It's remarkable, Thoreau says, how easily and quietly we fall into a route and "make a beaten track for ourselves." Before long his own feet had worn a path from his door down to the water. Even in a life chosen on purpose, a groove forms, and a groove can become a rut. Fourth, what he leaves out. Nothing says the cabin had gone stale or the experiment had failed. He could not spare more time for that one life, because others were waiting. The pond didn't fail him. He just had more lives to get to.

1246.title: A night in jail
1246.hook: he spent a night in jail for refusing a tax that supported slavery and the Mexican War
1246.carry: refusing to fund injustice, and paying the cost
1246.howItsDone: Readers often remember Thoreau's night in jail as a small, personal refusal: one person declining to fund what he saw as wrong, and accepting the cost quietly.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was why he left: as good a reason as he went, because he had several more lives to live. Your line was several more lives.

An ordinary errand. One summer afternoon Thoreau walks from the pond into Concord to pick up a shoe from the cobbler. Somewhere between the cabin and the shoe, he's stopped, arrested and locked in the town jail. No fight, no escape. He tells it in Walden almost in passing, in the chapter called The Village, as if it were weather. But that one night became the seed of an essay that would travel a long way.
screen: `A SHOE AT THE COBBLER'S.` → `ARRESTED ON THE WAY.` → `A NIGHT IN THE TOWN JAIL.`

segments.voice: First, the reason. Thoreau had stopped paying a tax to the state. In Walden he says why, in one bitter phrase: he would not pay a tax to, or recognize the authority of, a state that bought and sold men, women and children like cattle. In his essay on the night, he names two things he wouldn't fund: slavery, and his country's war with Mexico. Second, where a just person belongs: "Under a government which imprisons any unjustly, the true place for a just man is also a prison." If people are held unjustly, a cell is honest company. Third, the view from inside. Looking at the thick stone walls and the iron door, he felt the state could only lock up his body; his thoughts went where they liked. His own town, seen through bars, looked strange, like traveling into a far country he'd never expected to see. Fourth, the morning. Someone stepped in and paid the tax, and he was let out. No speech. He joined a party picking huckleberries on a hill outside town, where, he says, the state was nowhere to be seen. One night, then berries. What he did with it next is tomorrow's story.
screen: `A TAX HE WOULDN'T PAY.` · `THE TRUE PLACE FOR A JUST MAN.` · `HIS TOWN LIKE A FAR COUNTRY.` · then, large: `THEN HUCKLEBERRIES.`
